# Noctie AI Review 2026: Free Trial, Price, and Best Alternative

This Noctie AI review answers the real search questions first: Noctie is worth it if you want a human-like chess bot to play on web, iPhone, or Android. It is not fully free: there is a 7-day free trial, then a paid plan. The dedicated Noctie pricing page currently lists €14 monthly or €8 per month on the yearly plan, billed as €96 for the year. If you want a coach that explains, in plain language, why the move lost and lets you keep asking follow-ups on the same board, that's the Chessvia vs Noctie difference this page is about. [...] ### What is the best Noctie alternative?

Depends what you're after. Want another realistic opponent? The built-in bots on Chess.com and Lichess are worth a look, though they feel less human. Want the why behind your losses instead? Chessvia plays like a coach. It tells you, in plain words, why a move failed, and you can ask follow-ups on the same board.

### Does Chessvia explain moves like Noctie?

It goes further. Noctie grades your move with a quality label and a color. Chessvia explains, in words, why the move lost, and you can push back and ask again on the exact position until it makes sense. That two-way, plain-language why is the core of what Chessvia does, and it's the thing Noctie's own users most often say is missing.

### How current is this pricing comparison? [...] ### How much is Noctie AI?

In euros, not dollars. It's EUR 14 a month, or EUR 8 a month on the annual plan, which comes to EUR 96 for the year. For comparison, Chessvia's entry Silver tier is $7 a month, about $5 a month on annual billing. The currencies and the plan contents differ, so treat it as a product decision, not a price one.

### How does Noctie work?

You play a bot tuned to feel human, anywhere from beginner up toward grandmaster. It copies human openings, human mistakes, even human timing. Each move you make gets a color-coded grade, and you can take one back and ask for a hint. Your misses turn into puzzle decks, and there's opening and endgame drilling on the side.

But I open the coaching interface, and here I am faced with another simple program that is trying to get me to memorize moves, ruining the love I have for the game, tarnishing chess’s reputation as a strategic game in my mind.

Here’s what happened.

## Noctie.ai’s “Alternative Solution”

We have here my first experience: “the alternative solution.” I make a so-so move while the AI’s queen and bishop are putting pressure on my queen’s side. I move my queen’s pawn to d3, looking to remove pressure on what has been habitually a weak c2 pawn. There you go: strategy, flawed but present strategy. The bishop was putting pressure, and I’m reducing the pressure.
